The graph $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of three line segments. Then,

${\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide the interval of integration into $4$ regions: the line segment for $x\in [-6,-4],$ the line segment for $x\in [-4,-3),$ the line segment for $x\in [-3,0),$ and the line segment for $x\in [0,5].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-6}^{-4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-4}^{-3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{4}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-6,-4].$   The corresponding region is a triangle below the $x$-axis, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot 2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
{\int }_{-6}^{-4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-2.
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-3).$   The corresponding region is a triangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,0).$   The corresponding region is a rectangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =bh \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,5].$   The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3+1)(5) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2}+{A}_{3}+{A}_{4} \\  & =-2+\frac{1}{2}+6+10 \\  & =\frac{29}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

${\int }_{-4}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide the interval of integration into $3$ regions: the horizontal segment for $x\in [-4,-1],$ the sloped segment for $x\in (-1,0],$ and the sloped segment for $x\in [0,3].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-1}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-1].$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =bh \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (-1,0].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle below the $x$-axis, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we subtract its area.

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,3].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(bh) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot 3) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =6-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

${\int }_{-6}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We divide the interval of integration into $3$ regions: the arc of the semi-circle for $x\in [-6,-2],$ the line segment for $x\in [-2,2),$ and the line segment for $x\in (2,6].$ Using the additive property of integrals, we write

$$
{\int }_{-6}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-6}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-2}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{3}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-6,-2].$ The corresponding region is an upper semi-circle of radius $2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi (2)^{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,2).$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}4\cdot 4 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-8.
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (2,6].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4+1)\cdot 4 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{3}=-10.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}-{A}_{3} \\  & =2\pi -8-10 \\  & =2\pi -18.\end{aligned}
$$

Given the graph of $y=f(x)$ above, find the value of 
${\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph consists of $3$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [-4,-2]$, the arc of the semi-circle for $x\in [-2,2),$ and the line segment for $x\in (2,4].$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-2}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{2}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-2].$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =bh \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,2).$ The corresponding region is a combination of an inverted semi-circle of radius $2$ and a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =bh-\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =4(3)-\frac{1}{2}\pi (2)^{2} \\  & =12-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in (2,4].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =6+12-2\pi +3 \\  & =21-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14284587/assets/ad45cbdcd126df931f1a35c60ca12b45d520a2a0a5cddf4fa012c0515d3024c7.png)

The graph of $y=f(x),$ shown above, consists of two line segments. Find the value of $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The graph consists of two parts: the line segment for $x \in [0,2)$ and the line segment for $x \in [2,4].$ Therefore, we can write the required integral as follows:

$$
\int_{0}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = \underbrace{\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\int_{2}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x}_{-A_2}.
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in [0,2).$ The corresponding region is a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =bh \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in [2,4].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
\int_{2}^{4} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x =-A_2 = -2.
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2} \\  & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14284587/assets/36c6a1c84e0b0c32a5fd35fd422645f60340da6d205dd8cc31054cd558c2f5f9.png)

Given the graph of $y=f(x)$ above, find the value of $\displaystyle \int_{-4}^4 f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The graph consists of four parts: the arc of a semi-circle for $x\in [-4,0],$ a line segment for $x\in (0,2),$ a line segment for $x\in (2,4],$ and the point at $x=2.$ So, we can use the additive property of integrals to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={{{\int }_{-4}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+0+{{{\int }_{2}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in [-4,0].$ The corresponding region is a semi-circle with a radius of $2,$ so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \pi \cdot {2}^{2} \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in (0,2).$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\: \textrm{d}x = -A_2 = -2.
$$

- The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \in (2,4].$  The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}+{A}_{3} \\  & =2\pi -2+2 \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
The additive properties of integrals are beneficial when we have to integrate a piecewise function, such as 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14284587/assets/faef3f4c19469187aa3f4c2beb7a112005a761d2cc100b725b1b507fb34cac95.svg)

For example, let's calculate the integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int_{-5}^4 f(x) \,\textrm{d}x.
$$

We can split the integral into two integrals using the additive property, one integral for each "piece" of the piecewise function.

- The first integral will be over the integral $[-5,0],$ and

- the second integral will be over the integral $[0,4].$

Doing this, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-5}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-5}^{0}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{4}5\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{|}_{-5}^{0}+5x{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[{0}^{2}-(-5)^{2}]+5[4-0] \\  & =-\frac{25}{2}+20 \\  & =\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
